key_terms.meaning: The path command → linkage → surface deflection → airload → aircraft motion; break any link and the aircraft stops obeying the pilot.
The aerodynamic torque about a control surface's hinge line, in newton-metres (N·m); it is what the pilot or actuator must overcome.
A stiff tube that carries a command in compression as well as tension, so it needs guides and lost-motion-free joints.
Steel cables in matched pairs running over pulleys; each cable carries only tension, so a return path is compulsory.
An adjustable threaded link that sets and holds cable tension so both cables of a pair stay taut.
A pivoted lever that changes the direction of a rod or cable run and can also change the mechanical advantage.
A system that keeps the mechanical link and adds a hydraulic boost, so the pilot feels a reduced share of the hinge moment.
A system where actuators alone move the surface; the mechanical link is gone and artificial feel must be added.
A powered control whose actuator will not back-drive the cockpit, so surface loads are never felt by the pilot directly.
An artificial feel unit that makes stick force proportional to dynamic pressure q = ½ρV², imitating the feel of a mechanical aircraft.
A small tab whose deflection creates a hinge moment that moves the main surface, so the pilot moves the tab and the tab moves the surface.
A tab geared to move the same way as the surface, giving a stabilator positive stick force and preventing over-control.
A system where pilot inputs become electrical signals to computers that command hydraulic or electric actuators.
The software rule that converts pilot demand and sensor data into surface commands, shaping gain with speed, altitude and configuration.
Several computers and sensor lanes compute together and a majority vote rejects a faulty lane, so one failure does not change the command.
FBW whose signal path is optical fibre instead of wire, giving immunity to electromagnetic interference and no conductive path for lightning.
A closed loop that compares commanded with measured attitude or path and drives the servos itself, without the pilot's hand.
A servo loop that moves the throttle levers to hold a commanded speed, thrust or Mach number.
Use of the flight control system for load alleviation, flutter suppression, ride smoothing and relaxed static stability, not just pilot following.
Full Authority Digital Engine Control: a digital computer with full authority over fuel flow and engine geometry, replacing hydro-mechanical scheduling.

takeaways: An aircraft is not naturally stable in the sense the pilot wants, so a control chain must connect cockpit demand to aerodynamic response.
Rods carry push and pull; cables carry pull only, so cable systems always run in matched pairs with turnbuckles to keep tension.
Mechanical systems are simple and cheap but heavy, friction-ridden and hard to route through a large fuselage.
Above a certain size and speed the hinge moment exceeds human strength, so hydraulics supplies the force and the pilot supplies only the command.
An irreversible powered system must be given artificial feel, by a Q-feel unit or by tabs, or the pilot loses all sense of airspeed.
Fly-by-wire replaces mechanical linkage with computers and control laws, giving weight saving, envelope protection and carefree handling at the cost of redundancy.
An autopilot is the same control loop as the pilot's hand but closed by sensors and servos, and the auto throttle closes the same loop on the engine.
Active control technology turns the control surfaces into load and stability devices, allowing a smaller tail and a lighter wing.
Engine control is a separate loop: from throttle demand to fuel flow and geometry, now run digitally by FADEC inside every limit.
bank_note: Long answers here are usually built around one chain — command, linkage or signal, actuator, surface, airload — plus the reasons a given system replaced the previous one, so draw the block diagram and then justify each block.

bank.q: Explain why an aircraft needs a flight control system at all. Describe the chain from cockpit input to aircraft motion and name the quantity each link must handle.
outline: Aircraft does not hold a wanted attitude or path by itself; disturbances and trim changes act continuously
Chain: pilot command → linkage or signal → surface deflection → change in local angle of attack → aerodynamic force and hinge moment → aircraft motion
Feedback to the pilot through feel, or through sensors in a powered system
Distinguish control (short-term attitude) from trim and from stability

bank.q: Compare the push-pull rod system with the cable-pulley system for primary flight controls: construction, load paths, friction, weight and maintenance.
outline: Rod: tube in tension and compression, needs guides and bell cranks, high stiffness, low stretch, heavier over long runs
Cable: tension only, always in matched pairs, pulleys, turnbuckles, fairleads, follow-up on both sides
Friction and backlash: pulleys and swaging add compliance; rods add many joints
Routing through fuselage and wing, thermal expansion, preload, inspection for fraying or rod end wear
Which suits a small trainer and which suits a large transport

bank.q: List the main components of a conventional flight control system and state the function of each.
outline: Cockpit controls: stick or wheel, pedals, throttle
Linkage: rods, cables, pulleys, bell cranks, quadrants, turnbuckles
Surface attachments: horns, hinges, control surface itself
Feel and trim devices: trim tabs, bungees, downsprings, Q-feel unit
Stops, locks and gust locks; position indicators

bank.q: Explain the Q-feel system. Why is it needed, how does it work, and how does it produce stick force proportional to dynamic pressure?
outline: Irreversible powered control gives no hinge moment feedback to the pilot
q = ½ρV²; at higher speed and altitude-corrected speed the aircraft responds more sharply, so feel must rise too
Q-feel unit uses airspeed or impact pressure to load a spring or bungee in the linkage
Result: stick force per unit deflection rises with q, restoring natural handling and preventing over-stress
Compare with aerodynamic feel from a tab

bank.q: What is a servo tab? Explain how a small tab force moves a large surface, and how the anti-servo tab differs.
outline: Tab hinged at the trailing edge of the main surface
Pilot moves the tab; tab deflection creates a hinge moment about the main surface hinge
Main surface follows, so pilot force depends on tab size and gearing, not on surface area
Anti-servo tab moves same direction as surface, adding feel and damping on stabilators
Trim tab is set to a fixed deflection to relieve steady stick force

bank.q: Describe a digital fly-by-wire system. Explain the signal path and the role of control laws and redundancy.
outline: Pilot input transducers, air data and inertial sensors feed the flight control computers
Computers run control laws; output drives electro-hydraulic or electro-mechanical actuators
Control law gives gain scheduling with q and configuration, envelope protection, turn coordination
Redundancy: multiple computers, lanes, dissimilar hardware and software, majority voting, reversion modes
Advantages: weight, no rigging or friction, envelope protection; disadvantages: cost, software certification, power dependence

bank.q: Explain the operation of an autopilot and of an auto throttle, and state the advantages of each.
outline: Autopilot: sensor measures attitude or path, comparator forms error against command, computer shapes correction, servo moves surface
Inner loops (pitch rate, roll rate) and outer loops (altitude, heading); PID shaping for damping
Modes: wing level, heading hold, altitude hold, glide slope and localiser tracking, autoland
Auto throttle: servo drives throttle levers to hold speed, thrust or Mach; coupled to autopilot in approach
Advantages: reduced workload, fuel saving, precise tracking, consistent approach speed, better ride

bank.q: Explain full authority digital engine control (FADEC). How does it replace a hydro-mechanical fuel control unit?
outline: Engine loop: throttle lever angle in, fuel flow and geometry (VSV, VBV, bleed) out, thrust produced
Sensors: N1, N2, EGT, fuel flow, inlet pressure and temperature, PLA
Hydro-mechanical unit uses cams and bellows to schedule fuel against speed and pressure
FADEC: digital schedule with full authority, limits on N and EGT, start and reverse scheduling, built-in test
Advantages: fuel efficiency, precise limits, condition monitoring; needs redundant channels and power

bank.q: A transport aircraft of 60 t has a control surface with hinge moment coefficient 0.08, area 2.4 m² and chord 0.5 m. Estimate the hinge moment at 250 m/s at sea level and decide whether a human could move it without hydraulic boost. Show each step.
outline: q = ½ρV² with ρ = 1.225 kg/m³ gives about 38 kPa
Hinge moment = Ch × q × S × c
Substitute and get the number with units (N·m)
Compare with a realistic stick force through the linkage and with a human limit of a few hundred newtons
Conclude that full power or power assist is needed; state assumptions about deflection

bank.q: A small trainer has irreversible controls only on the elevator. Explain how you would add artificial feel and how you would trim it, using only tabs and bungees.
outline: Elevator feel: bungee or spring cartridge in the linkage, plus a downspring if needed for static stability
Anti-servo tab on stabilator to give positive stick force gradient
Trim: trim tab deflection relieves steady stick force, or an adjustable spring in the circuit
Check that force per unit speed rises and that trim authority covers the CG range
State the consequence of no feel: over-control and structural risk

bank.q: Design the redundancy scheme for a digital fly-by-wire flight control computer of a civil transport and justify the voting scheme you choose.
outline: Three or four computers, two lanes each; dissimilar software and hardware
Sensor lanes duplicated; comparison, threshold and majority vote (2-out-of-3 or 3-out-of-4)
Fail-passive first, then fail-operational after further failures
Reversion modes, direct law versus normal law, degradation announcement
Power supply redundancy, built-in test, maintenance significance
Certification argument and probability of loss of control

bank.q: Compare mechanical, power-assisted, fully powered and fly-by-wire flight control systems on weight, feel, redundancy, maintenance and envelope protection. Which suits a 2-seat trainer and which suits a large transport?
outline: Weight trend with aircraft size and run length
Feel: natural, boosted, artificial by Q-feel, artificial by control law
Redundancy: none, simple, duplicated hydraulics, multi-computer systems
Maintenance: rigging, backlash, hydraulic leaks versus software and LRU replacement
Envelope protection only in FBW; cost and certification burden
Recommendation map: trainer to mechanical or simple powered; transport to FBW

bank.q: Discuss active control technology. How do load alleviation, flutter suppression, gust alleviation and relaxed static stability change the aircraft design, and what risks does each introduce?
outline: Gust and manoeuvre load alleviation reduces wing bending moment, allowing a lighter wing
Flutter suppression extends the speed envelope with a smaller tail
Relaxed static stability allows a smaller tail and better cruise efficiency at the cost of continuous computer involvement
Ride smoothing for passenger comfort
Risks: dependence on the control system, failure cases, software maturity, pilot training
Carefree handling as an operational benefit

bank.q: Evaluate fly-by-light against fly-by-wire. State the physical reasons for its advantages and the practical reasons it is not universal.
outline: FBW signal path is electrical wire; FBL uses optical fibre
Advantages: no electromagnetic interference, no conductive path for lightning or high intensity radiated fields, lower cable weight, higher bandwidth
Problems: optical connectors and splices are delicate, bend radius limits routing, actuators still need electrical power, optical to hydraulic interface adds complexity
Weight of copper against weight of fibre and terminations
Where FBL suits: military and high-interference environments

bank.q: An aircraft on approach shows a slow pitch oscillation after the autopilot was engaged. Analyse the possible causes in the control loop and the checks you would make.
outline: Identify loop elements: sensor, comparator, control law gain and damping, servo, surface, aircraft dynamics
Sensor error or lag; altitude or pitch sensor noise
Control law gain too high for current q; scheduled gain fault
Servo rate limit or backlash; actuator hysteresis
Aircraft handling changes with speed and configuration; CG shift
Test: disengage, check in manual, check gain schedule and servo rigging

bank.q: Modern aircraft group flight control, autopilot, engine and navigation functions into integrated modular avionics. Discuss the benefits and the new failure modes this creates.
outline: LRUs replaced by common computing modules hosting software partitions
Benefits: weight, power, cost, fewer connectors, easier upgrade, shared maintenance data
Partitioning and robust time and space separation; certification of shared resources
New failure modes: common mode failure in shared modules, network and bus failures, software complexity, thermal loading
Redundancy and grace degradation; maintenance and built-in test implications
Flight management system and autopilot coupling through a shared data bus

glossary.def: A movable aerofoil whose deflection changes the force or moment on the aircraft, such as an aileron, elevator, rudder or flap.
The pitch control surface hinged to the horizontal tailplane, moving the tail lift thus the pitching moment.
A wing trailing-edge surface deflected differentially to produce roll; one goes up while the other goes down.
The yaw control surface on the vertical fin, producing side force and yaw, also used to coordinate turns.
A one-piece horizontal tail whose whole surface moves about a pivot, used instead of a separate fin and elevator.
A small steady deflection or force that holds the aircraft in the desired state without continuous pilot input.
A small hinged tab set to a fixed deflection that produces a steady hinge moment to relieve stick force in cruise.
The lever arm on a control surface to which the push-pull rod or cable is attached, setting the mechanical advantage.
Lost motion between linked parts, so a small control input produces no output; it adds free play and can cause flutter.
q = ½ρV², in pascals when ρ is kg/m³ and V is m/s; it sets the aerodynamic force on a surface and hence the feel force.
The ratio of output force to input force of a linkage, the inverse of the ratio of their displacements.
A device that compares a command with a measured position and drives an output until the error is removed.
A valve that meters hydraulic flow in proportion to a small electrical current, giving fast, precise actuator control.
The hydraulic or electric ram that converts a command signal into a force and stroke on a control surface.
A control system in which pilot input is converted to electrical signals and computers command the actuators.
Control-law limiting that prevents the aircraft exceeding angle of attack, load factor, pitch or bank limits whatever the pilot asks.
A degraded FBW mode where pilot inputs pass to the surfaces with simple gearing and no envelope protection.
A system that holds or tracks an attitude, heading, altitude or path by closing the control loop through sensors and servos.
A servo system that drives the throttles automatically to hold a selected speed, thrust or Mach number.
A design where the aircraft is deliberately made slightly unstable and stabilised continuously by the flight control system.
Deflecting surfaces automatically to reduce wing or tail bending loads during gusts and manoeuvres.
Line Replaceable Unit: a box that can be swapped on the flight line without recalibration or deep maintenance.
Full Authority Digital Engine Control: a redundant digital computer that schedules engine fuel and geometry within all limits.
The position of the cockpit thrust lever, the command input to the engine control loop, usually given in degrees.
